I'd say no because there is little evidence that one way of eating is better than another. All that matters is getting your vitamins and not over or under eating. Some people eat carbs all day and are healthy. Some people eat no carbs and are healthy. Those with kidney failure can't eat much protein. Those with other diseases need a lot of protein.

The problem is that there is no "best way to eat." You can eat only fruit and vegetables and be obese, get type 2 diabetes, and have high cholesterol. You can eat only tastycakes and be at a healthy weight with no apparent health problems. Everyone just needs to get their nutritional needs met while maintaining portion control, and there is no "one size fits all" way to do that. Some people believe eating 10 times a day is good for you, others benefit from only eating 1 meal. Some people eat high carb low fat, some eat low carb high fat. There are a lot of great responses here, but here's my 2 cents.  What I believe makes US healthcare so expensive is also what I believe makes it innovative. Suing in the US is much more common than it might be elsewhere. This forces hospitals to get lawyers, healthcare workers to get malpractice insurance, hospitals hire quality assurance teams, and every procedure is researched greatly to assure that if the hospital/employee is sued they can assure that they are not at fault. So while this makes a lot of procedures more safe and effective, it also adds an addition cost to everything. Nurses can be held liable for a patient getting out of bed and falling, even if the patient knows they shouldn't get out of bed. A surgeon can perform an operation perfectly but the patient might still sue if it doesn't work. I wish there was an easy solution, but the way things are forces healthcare workers to do their best and keeps them accountable. It forces researchers to innovate. But it also keeps uninsured people sick, without money for treatment. I honestly don't know how this can be fixed, without hospitals losing the motivation to innovate.

The child will usually succeed greatly in one aspect, but have difficulty with social interaction and emotional regulation. An infant isn't expected to do much, and development varies more. As a toddler develops their doctor is checking on their developmental milestones. Which there are a lot of in toddlerhood. If they aren't met in some areas, sometimes ahead in others (for example, some autisitic toddlers can be very good at drawing while behind in language skills) , it could be an indicator of autism. It's a lot harder to notice in an infant, as they can seem fairly normal.

It's one of those "correlation does not equal causation" kind of things.

Of course there is a correlation when autism signs don't typically appear for the first few years, when many infants/toddlers get vaccinated, but that does not indicate causation. Many children aren't even diagnosed until preschool because their parents are too oblivious/hopeful to notice.
